newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Euro central bank might seek guidance from FX rates.
newsitem.headline: Euro central bank might seek guidance from FX rates.

text.p: A future European Central Bank may well have to set a value for the new single currency against the dollar in order to steer monetary policy during the early stages of a common currency, analysts say.

While the issue is no doubt controversial and unlikely to receive any official commentary, such an option is perceived as one of the best ways -- some argue the only way -- for the ECB to gauge the credibility of its initial policy decisions.

At issue are the tools the new central bank will use in making monetary policy and its ability to convince financial markets that it will be tough on inflation. The European Monetary Institute, forerunner to the ECB, will unveil its blueprint for the new central bank's policy instruments on Friday in Frankfurt.

The analyssts said that without recourse to many of the national economic indicators central bankers normally use to implement policy, the ECB may have to lean on the exchange rate between the euro and the dollar as an informational tool.
Money supply measures, for example, might be less than reliable at start of monetary union, they said.
"All the usual indicators will be unreliable. The only thing you can rely on is the exchange rate," says Guenther Thumann, economist at Salomon Brothers in London.
Indeed, some experts say the strategy is actively under consideration among EU officials.

On a recent visit to Europe, Princeton University economist Peter Kenen said he detected that such an approach was being discussed as a way of establishing the ECB's credibility with financial markets.

"How does the ECB establish its inflation credentials if there is no inflation," Kenen asked. "One way is to adopt an exchange rate target and make sure the euro doesn't depreciate against the dollar."

Embracing an exchange rate target carries risks, however, not least of which is the contractionary effect it might have on economic growth. Too restrictive a policy, combined with tight budgets across the single currency area, could aggravate the already poor employment situation in Europe.
Analysts say such concerns may be behind France's desire to have a political body to counterbalance the independence of the ECB.
At a summit of EU leaders in Dublin last month there was a clear rift between Germany and France over the extent to which the ECB would be allowed a free hand in setting monetary policy.

Germany, strongly wedded to the importance of price stability, wants the central bank to have as much freedom from political intereference as possible. France, meanwhile, believes ECB decisions should be taken within the context of broader economic objectives such as employment.

"My real concern is that if the ECB is left to its own devices it would pursue a policy that is inappropriately tight," said Kenen, adding that such a development could potentially undermine public confidence in the entire project.
Another problem with using a euro/dollar rate is the quality of the information it would convey at the start of monetary union, in particular what it may have to say about U.S. economic policy.
"The exchange rate is a relative phenomenon and you would have to disentangle the U.S. policy impact," said an EU monetary official.

"Another problem is that there may be portfolio shifts which could be difficult to separate from the messages sent by the market," he added. "I would say the impact on long-term yields would be much more important in assessing credibility."

Nevertheless, advocates argue the exchange rate would offer monetary authorities instantaneous feedback about the appropriateness of their policy decisions and would be in keeping with the past practices of other central banks.
Economists noted that the Bundesbank has itself occasionally used the dollar/mark rate as a guide to future policy decisions, even though officially such a strategy would never be acknowledged.
